text: Every mechanic this course has covered — batching, collision resolution, a clean commit, solid ATF coverage, a green pipeline run — can be executed flawlessly, and a scoped application can still deploy with zero defects and cause real business disruption. Deployment planning is also a sequencing question, a timing question, and a communication question, and skipping any one of the three changes what 'it deployed cleanly' actually means.

Chapter 2 covered why Update Sets that depend on each other have to promote in the correct order. A scoped application has the same problem at a larger scale. If it depends on a shared script include, a plugin, or a separate application that isn't active yet on the target instance, deploying it first doesn't fail loudly. It can activate successfully and then break the first time a real user triggers the feature that needed that missing piece. Map every real dependency first.

A build being ready isn't the same as it being the right moment to deploy it. Before committing to a time, check two real tools: the Change Calendar, a visual view of everything already scheduled on the target instance for that window, and Conflict Detection, which automatically flags a planned change that overlaps in time with another change touching the same Configuration Item. Confirming both is a different risk profile than deploying whenever the pipeline goes green.

A real deployment plan answers three questions before it ever runs: sequencing — what has to already be in place on the target instance, and in what order; timing — when, specifically, is this actually safe, confirmed against the Change Calendar and Conflict Detection; and communication — who needs to know beforehand, and exactly how will they be told.

Perfect sequencing and a genuinely low-traffic window can still cause a support-ticket storm if nobody told the people who use the application. A short heads-up that a feature will be briefly unavailable, or will look different afterward, isn't a courtesy layered on top of the plan — it's part of what makes the deployment succeed from the business's point of view, not just the platform's. A user who hits an unexpected change mid-task with no warning will treat it as an outage, no matter how clean the deployment was underneath.

Sequencing, timing, communication — a plan that only maps dependency order is a technical checklist, not a deployment plan. Next lesson: what to actually do when, despite all that planning, a deployment still goes wrong, and how a real team decides between reverting it entirely and fixing it forward.
